category: Commercial Voice Overlap Profiles - Final Batch

profiles.name: Duane Thompson
profiles.excerpt: Duane Thompson moved from silent-film leading lady and stage work into radio, where Hollywood Hotel and Lux Radio Theatre made her microphone career more than a postscript to the silent era.
profiles.bio_html:
Duane Thompson, born Lura Duane Malony in Iowa in 1903, entered motion pictures in the silent era and became one of the WAMPAS Baby Stars of 1925. The transition to sound narrowed her film opportunities, but it did not end her performing career. She worked in stock theatre and then found a durable place in radio.

Radio gave Thompson a new kind of visibility. She became the telephone-operator voice that opened Hollywood Hotel with its familiar greeting, and she worked in comedy as well as dramatic repertory. On Lux Radio Theatre, surviving source records repeatedly place her in both dramatic doubling and sponsor presentation, a practical combination that shows how experienced studio actors moved between story and advertising inside the same broadcast.

Golden Radio Hour currently verifies Thompson on 13 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts. The underlying credit record includes repeated commercial-spokesman or commercial-spokeswoman work, so GRH treats sponsor performance as a genuine secondary part of her radio career rather than an isolated tag.

profiles.name: Ann Tobin
profiles.excerpt: Ann Tobin was one of Lux Radio Theatre’s recurring studio performers, appearing in dramatic support and in the sponsor material that helped hold the weekly anthology together.
profiles.bio_html:
Ann Tobin is one of the radio professionals whose surviving broadcast credits are stronger than the surviving personal publicity. Golden Radio Hour therefore treats the work itself as the center of her profile instead of filling gaps with unsupported biography.

Tobin appears repeatedly in Lux Radio Theatre, where Goldin catalogue records identify her not only among the supporting company but specifically as a commercial spokesman on multiple broadcasts. That repeated sponsor work matters because it shows she was trusted with the advertising portion of one of network radio’s most prominent sponsored dramas, not merely handed a single stray commercial line.

Golden Radio Hour currently verifies Tobin on 15 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and one Voyage of the Scarlet Queen performance. Her preserved Lux work includes repeated sponsor credits, making Commercial Voices & Sponsor Performers an appropriate secondary category while her primary identity remains actor.

profiles.name: Vicki Vola
profiles.excerpt: Vicki Vola was a major radio professional whose long run as Edith Miller on Mr. District Attorney led into decades of broadcast acting and national leadership of AFTRA.
profiles.bio_html:
Victoria Vola began broadcasting as a teenager at Denver station KLZ in 1932, after early study in music, dance and theatre. She worked on the West Coast before moving east in 1938 and establishing herself in the competitive New York radio industry, where steady employment made her one of the medium’s busiest working actors.

Her best-known role was Edith Miller, secretary to the title character on Mr. District Attorney. Vola carried the part from radio into television and continued working in later audio drama, including Theater Five and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar. Her career also had an institutional side: after years of union service she became AFTRA’s national president from 1963 to 1965, the organization’s second elected woman president.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Mr. District Attorney performances, 17 Theater Five episodes, four Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, three Quiet Please appearances, two CBS Radio Mystery Theater episodes and two Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances. A commercial tag survives in the archive metadata, but the evidence is too isolated to make sponsor performance a public secondary category.

profiles.name: Veola Vonn
profiles.excerpt: Veola Vonn was a radio actress and singer whose comedy work included The Great Gildersleeve and The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show before a broader film and television career.
profiles.bio_html:
Veola Vonn, sometimes credited as Vyola Vonn, was born in New York City in 1918 and worked as an actress and singer across radio, film and television. Her screen career began in the 1930s, but radio remained an important part of her professional life.

Vonn worked alongside prominent radio comedians and character actors, including her husband Hanley Stafford, and appeared on programs ranging from Blondie to The Great Gildersleeve. Her surviving GRH record is strongest in comedy, where her voice joined established ensemble casts rather than being tied to one famous continuing character.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine The Great Gildersleeve performances, four The Phil Harris-Alice Faye Show appearances, two The Railroad Hour episodes and work on Duffy’s Tavern. One isolated Lux commercial tag is retained in the research data but is not enough to classify Vonn publicly as a commercial voice.

profiles.name: Regina Wallace
profiles.excerpt: Regina Wallace was a dependable West Coast radio actress whose surviving work is concentrated in Lux Radio Theatre, where she supported major stars in weekly film adaptations.
profiles.bio_html:
Regina Wallace is best documented through the broadcast record rather than through a large body of surviving personal biography. That record places her inside the Los Angeles repertory system that supplied Lux Radio Theatre with experienced supporting voices around each week’s featured stars.

Wallace could be entrusted with named dramatic parts as well as smaller ensemble work. In the 1944 Lux adaptation of Shadow of a Doubt, for example, she played Mrs. Newton opposite William Powell and Teresa Wright. Other Lux records place her among the supporting company across wartime and postwar productions.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 18 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and one Dr. Christian performance for Wallace. Sponsor-role metadata also appears in the source data, but the public evidence is not strong enough to make commercial presentation a defining secondary category, so GRH keeps the profile centered on her verified acting work.

profiles.name: Justina Wayne
profiles.excerpt: Justina Wayne was a recurring Lux Radio Theatre studio performer whose surviving credits show the kind of dependable supporting work that weekly prestige radio required.
profiles.bio_html:
Justina Wayne survives in the historical record primarily through program documentation rather than through extensive biographical publicity. Golden Radio Hour keeps that distinction clear: her page is built around what the broadcasts verify, not around invented personal detail.

Wayne appears repeatedly in Lux Radio Theatre during the program’s early Hollywood years. Goldin catalogue entries place her among the supporting company in productions such as One Sunday Afternoon and She Loves Me Not, alongside the rotating stars, doubles, announcers, musicians and commercial performers who made the weekly anthology possible.

Golden Radio Hour currently verifies Wayne on ten Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts. An isolated sponsor-role tag remains preserved in the source metadata for future checking, but it is not sufficient evidence to promote her into the public Commercial Voices & Sponsor Performers category.

profiles.name: Martha Wentworth
profiles.excerpt: Martha Wentworth was one of radio’s great utility actresses, a performer of extraordinary vocal range whose career stretched from early broadcasting through crime drama, comedy and animation.
profiles.bio_html:
Verna Martha Wentworth was born in New York City in 1889 and trained for the stage before radio became a major part of her working life. By the early 1920s she was already building the kind of microphone versatility that later earned her the nickname “Actress of 100 Voices.”

Wentworth’s radio range was unusually broad. She played the Wintergreen Witch in The Cinnamon Bear, worked in crime and anthology drama, appeared repeatedly on comedy programs and became the sort of repertory performer who could disappear into sharply different voices from one production to the next. That same flexibility later carried into animation, including Disney voice work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 29 The Red Skelton Show performances, 17 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, eight Broadway Is My Beat appearances, six Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar episodes and additional work on The Whistler, Calling All Cars and western programs. A single Lux sponsor tag is retained in the source layer but does not define her public category.

profiles.name: Walter White
profiles.excerpt: Walter White is preserved by Golden Radio Hour as a supporting radio performer on Lux Radio Theatre and Calling All Cars, with the biography deliberately limited to credits that can be securely tied to this identity.
profiles.bio_html:
The name Walter White creates a genuine identification problem in radio research because it is shared with better-documented public figures whose broadcasts can be mixed into generic performer indexes. Golden Radio Hour therefore does not attach unrelated life history to this actor without evidence.

The GRH archive does securely connect this Walter White to a run of Lux Radio Theatre productions from the late 1930s into 1940 and to an earlier Calling All Cars appearance. That pattern is consistent with a working supporting performer in the Hollywood radio pool, but the surviving record does not justify claims about childhood, education, family or a broader screen career.

Golden Radio Hour currently verifies nine Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and one Calling All Cars performance for this identity. A sponsor-role tag is preserved for later verification, but it is not promoted into a public commercial-voice category.

profiles.name: June Whitley
profiles.excerpt: June Whitley brought Canadian stage and CBC experience to Hollywood radio, where she became the original Margaret Anderson opposite Robert Young on Father Knows Best.
profiles.bio_html:
June Whitley, born June Culbertson in Vancouver, developed her acting experience in local theatre and on Canadian radio before moving to Hollywood in the late 1940s. Her CBC work included featured roles on programs such as Stage Party and Vancouver Theatre, giving her a professional radio foundation before she entered American network broadcasting.

Her most important radio role was Margaret Anderson, wife of Robert Young’s Jim Anderson on Father Knows Best. Whitley helped establish the family dynamic of the radio series before the property became far better known on television. She also worked across drama and crime programs rather than remaining confined to domestic comedy.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 15 Father Knows Best performances, 14 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, seven Dragnet appearances and additional work on Broadway Is My Beat, Philip Marlowe, The Railroad Hour and The Whistler. An isolated Lux sponsor tag remains in the source data but is not strong enough to define a public secondary category.

profiles.name: Paula Winslowe
profiles.excerpt: Paula Winslowe was a consummate working radio actress whose career joined character acting, dramatized advertising, Disney voice work and the long-running role of Peg Riley on The Life of Riley.
profiles.bio_html:
Paula Winslowe built her career around the value of a reliable voice. After early stage and dubbing work, she became busy at KHJ and the Don Lee network in Los Angeles, where local drama and national network programs created steady demand for actors who could move quickly between character parts and commercial copy.

Advertising was not incidental to Winslowe’s radio career. She performed dramatized commercials for the Woodbury program and became a familiar member of Lux Radio Theatre, where she could support the dramatic cast and sell the sponsor’s product in the same hour. Her larger acting career included Peg Riley on The Life of Riley, later anthology and detective work, and the voice of Bambi’s mother for Disney. She continued acting in radio into the Sears Radio Theater era.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts, 12 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances, ten Crime Classics episodes, seven Broadway Is My Beat appearances, seven Sears Radio Theater performances and additional work across major comedy and dramatic series. Her documented history of dramatized advertising makes Commercial Voices & Sponsor Performers a substantial secondary category.

profiles.name: Barbara Jean Wong
profiles.excerpt: Barbara Jean Wong began as a child radio performer, became one of the era’s notable Chinese American voices, and worked in both dramatic roles and Lux Radio Theatre sponsor presentation before a later career in education.
profiles.bio_html:
Barbara Jean Wong was born in Los Angeles in 1924 and began performing as a child. A fourth-generation Chinese American, she entered radio while still young and developed a career that included children’s fantasy, family comedy, mystery and network anthology work at a time when Asian American performers were given far fewer substantial opportunities than white actors.

Her radio credits included Judy Barton in The Cinnamon Bear, Arbadella on Amos ’n’ Andy, work connected with Charlie Chan and I Love a Mystery, and appearances on major anthology programs. Surviving Lux documentation also identifies Wong repeatedly in commercial-spokesman roles, so sponsor presentation was a real part of her microphone work rather than a one-off metadata accident.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and a The Halls of Ivy appearance for Wong. Her broader career later included film work, university study and a long second profession as an elementary-school teacher. GRH keeps the radio and sponsor history connected to that fuller life rather than reducing her to a single program credit.
